title: Severe bleeding
summary: Life-threatening bleeding: press hard, then tourniquet on an arm or leg, or pack the wound in the neck, armpit or groin.

steps.text: Make sure the scene is safe. Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.
steps.detail:
Your own safety comes first. If you get hurt you cannot help anyone. If the situation becomes unsafe, stop, move to safety, and take the casualty with you if you can.

Wear gloves if you have them. If blood gets on you, wash it off afterwards and tell a health care provider you were exposed.

Bleeding is the number one cause of preventable death after injury, so this protocol comes before almost everything else. If someone else is free, have them make the call or go for help while you start on the bleeding.

steps.text: Find where the blood is coming from. Open, cut or pull away clothing so you can see the wound.
steps.detail:
Clothing can soak up and hide a large amount of blood, and there may be more than one wound. Check the arms and legs, the neck, armpits and groin, and the body front and back.

Signs that bleeding is life-threatening: blood that keeps flowing steadily or spurts, a large amount of blood, blood pooling on the ground, or bleeding that will not stop when you press on it. As a rough guide, Stop the Bleed teaches that about half a can of soda (6 ounces) of blood loss, or a continuous steady flow, should be treated as serious. People are poor at judging blood volume, so if in doubt treat it as life-threatening.

Also treat it as life-threatening if the casualty becomes drowsy, dizzy, confused, or passes out.

If you see organs (such as bowel) showing through a belly wound, do not press on them or push them back: cover them loosely with a clean, moist dressing (see the warning on the next step).

steps.text: Press hard, directly on the bleeding spot, with gauze or clean cloth under your hands. Not on organs showing through a belly wound: see the warning.
steps.detail:
Put the pad right on the place the blood is coming from, not beside it, and push down hard with both hands. Lock your arms and lean your body weight onto it. Use just enough gauze or cloth to cover the wound; a big pile spreads your pressure out.

Direct pressure is the first step for bleeding almost anywhere on the body (the exception is organs showing through a belly wound), and it is what you do with your hands while someone gets a tourniquet or packing ready.

If you have no gauze or cloth, press with your gloved or bare hands. Do not waste time looking for the perfect dressing.

ask.q: Is the bleeding life-threatening (spurting, steady flow, pooling, or not slowing with hard pressure)?

steps.warn: Organs showing through a belly wound: do not press on them or push them back. Cover loosely with a clean, moist dressing.

steps.detail:
A tourniquet works only on an arm or leg, and only when it can go on above the wound, between the wound and the body.

Wounds in the neck, armpit, groin, or high on the thigh or shoulder where a tourniquet cannot go above the wound are called junctional wounds. They are treated by packing the wound and pressing hard.

Wounds of the chest, belly or back are handled differently; the next questions sort them out.

ask.q: Is the wound on an arm or leg, with room for a tourniquet above it?

steps.text: Put a tourniquet on 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over the elbow or knee. Tighten it until the bleeding stops.
steps.detail:
A manufactured tourniquet is the first choice for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, and it should go on as soon as possible. Place the band 2 to 3 inches above the wound, between the wound and the heart. Never place it over a joint. If you cannot see exactly where the bleeding is coming from, put it high on the limb.

Pull the strap tight, then turn the windlass rod (or work the ratchet) until the bleeding stops. Lock the rod in place. Military guidance applies it directly on the skin; Stop the Bleed notes it can go over clothes.

Tourniquets hurt. That is expected and does not mean it is wrong. Keep tightening until the bleeding stops.

Leave the tourniquet where everyone can see it. Do not cover it with clothing or a blanket. Write the time of application on the casualty's skin or the tourniquet. The app's tourniquet tool asks which limb, starts a timer and logs it.

Children: a manufactured windlass or ratchet tourniquet can be used on children from about 2 years old, or when the limb is about 5 inches (13 cm) around or more. For a baby or very small child where the tourniquet will not tighten, press hard directly on the wound instead (step 3), and pack large deep wounds the same way as adults.

No manufactured tourniquet: press hard on the wound (step 3) and keep pressing. Only if that fails, and only if you have been trained, consider an improvised tourniquet. Use a broad, flat band that does not stretch, at least 2 inches wide (a folded cravat or strip of clothing), twist it tight with a rigid stick or tool handle as a windlass, and tie the windlass so it cannot unwind. Improvised tourniquets fail often, so watch it closely. Do not use thin cord or wire: narrow bands cause more pain and tissue damage.
steps.warn: Do not loosen or remove a tourniquet to check the wound.

steps.text: Still bleeding? Tighten more. If it still bleeds, put a second tourniquet on side by side with the first.
steps.detail: A second tourniquet is needed when the first does not stop the bleeding, when bleeding starts again, or on a large or very muscular limb. Place it side by side with the first and tighten it until the bleeding stops. Log it with the tourniquet tool as well.

steps.text: Leave tourniquets on. Keep the casualty warm and watch for shock. Get them to medical care.
steps.detail:
Do not remove the tourniquet. Taking a tourniquet off or converting it to a dressing is an advanced procedure: use the Tourniquet reassessment and conversion protocol. Without someone trained to do that, leave it on and keep monitoring until the casualty reaches medical care.

Blood loss causes shock. Keep the casualty lying down, protect them from the cold ground and wind, and follow the Shock protocol.

Keep checking the wound below the tourniquet for new bleeding, and keep checking the rest of the body for wounds you missed.

steps.text: Neck, armpit, groin, or a deep arm or leg wound with no tourniquet: pack the wound. Push gauze or clean cloth deep into it until it is full.
steps.detail:
For a large or deep wound, pressing on the surface does not reach the bleeding. Packing puts the pressure where the blood is coming from.

How: find the bleeding spot inside the wound. Push the end of the gauze in with one or two fingers, right onto that spot. Keep feeding gauze in, pressing it down as you go, until the wound is packed tightly and no more will go in. If you run out of gauze, use clean cloth (a T-shirt, bandanna).

This works for deep wounds of the neck, armpits and groin, and for deep arm and leg wounds where a tourniquet is not available. It can be done on children the same way as adults.

Hemostatic (clotting) gauze is packed the same way and helps stop bleeding; use the Hemostatic gauze wound packing protocol. Plain gauze or cloth packed tightly with hard pressure still works.

steps.text: Press hard on the packed wound with both hands and do not let up until help takes over.
steps.detail:
Put both hands on top of the packing and push down with your body weight. Keep pressing. Stop the Bleed teaches holding pressure until help arrives.

If blood soaks through, do not pull the packing out. Press harder on the same spot, or pack more on top and press. Piling on more gauze is not a substitute for pressure.

If another person can take over, swap without releasing pressure: their hands go on as yours come off.

steps.text: Once the bleeding has stopped, wrap a pressure bandage firmly over the packing. Keep watching it and treat for shock.
steps.detail:
A pressure dressing (an elastic trauma bandage wrapped firmly) can hold the packing in and keep the bleeding stopped, which frees your hands. If bleeding starts again through the bandage, press directly on the wound again with your hands until it stops.

Pressure bandages or devices may be used when holding manual pressure is not possible, for example when you have to move the casualty or treat someone else.

Follow the Shock protocol: keep the casualty lying down and warm, and get them to medical care.

steps.text: Keep pressing until the bleeding stops, then wrap a firm bandage over the dressing.
steps.detail:
Most bleeding that is not life-threatening stops with steady direct pressure on the wound.

Once it has stopped, a pressure dressing can keep it stopped while you move. If bleeding comes back through the dressing, press directly on the wound again until it stops; do not just add more layers.

If at any point the bleeding becomes heavy, spurts, or will not stop with pressure, go back and treat it as life-threatening.

Organs showing through a belly wound (Red Cross): do not push them back in and do not press on them. Remove clothing from around the wound, wet clean dressings with clean warm water or saline, and lay them loosely over the wound; cover loosely with plastic wrap or foil if you have it. Lay the casualty on their back with knees bent unless that hurts (leave them as found if a head, neck or back injury is possible, unless you must move them). Keep them from getting cold or overheated, care for shock, and get them to medical care urgently.
steps.warn: Organs showing through a belly wound: do not press on them or push them back. Cover loosely with a clean, moist dressing.

steps.text: Is the wound in the neck, armpit or groin, or a deep arm or leg wound where a tourniquet cannot be used?
steps.detail:
Packing is the Stop the Bleed technique for deep wounds of the neck, armpits and groin, and for deep limb wounds when a tourniquet is not available or will not fit.

If the wound is on the chest, belly, back or elsewhere on the body, answer no.

ask.q: Neck, armpit, groin, or a deep limb wound with no tourniquet?

steps.text: Is the wound on the chest (front, side or back of the ribcage)?
steps.detail: A wound to the chest can let air into the space around the lung. It needs different handling from other body wounds.

ask.q: Is the wound on the chest?

steps.text: Chest wound: press firmly on the bleeding with gauze or cloth, but do not seal the hole airtight. Then use the Open chest wound protocol.
steps.detail:
Control heavy bleeding with direct pressure. Any dressing over a chest wound can trap air inside the chest (AHA/Red Cross 2024), so keep it loose and watch breathing.

Current first aid guidance (AHA and Red Cross 2024) is to leave an open chest wound open to the air or loosely covered with a clean dry dressing that does not seal. The Open chest wound protocol covers this step by step.

steps.text: Belly or other body wound: press hard and steadily on the bleeding with gauze or clean cloth, and keep pressing until help takes over.
steps.detail:
Direct manual pressure is the first treatment for life-threatening bleeding that a tourniquet cannot reach (AHA and Red Cross). Push down hard with both hands on the bleeding spot and do not let up.

If blood soaks through, press harder on the same spot rather than lifting the dressing. Once the bleeding has stopped, a firm pressure bandage can hold the dressing in place.

The Red Cross bleeding algorithm lists wound packing for head, neck and trunk wounds by trained responders. This app does not guide packing of belly or chest wounds; press instead.

Bleeding inside the belly cannot be controlled from outside. Follow the Shock protocol and get the casualty to medical care urgently.
steps.warn: If organs are showing, do not press on them or push them back. Cover them loosely with a clean, moist dressing.

steps.text: Are organs (such as bowel) showing through the wound?
steps.detail: With a deep belly wound, loops of bowel or other organs can push out through the opening. These must not be pressed on.

ask.q: Are organs showing through the wound?

steps.text: Organs showing: do not push them back or press on them. Cover loosely with a clean, moist dressing.
steps.detail:
Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

Remove clothing from around the wound. Do not push the organs back in and do not press on them.

Wet clean dressings (gauze or cloth) with clean, warm water or saline and lay them loosely over the wound and organs. If you have plastic wrap or aluminium foil, lay it loosely over the wet dressings.

Lay the casualty on their back with knees bent, unless that hurts. If a head, neck or back injury is possible, leave them as found unless you must move them for safety, CPR or to control bleeding.

Keep them from getting cold or overheated, give care for shock (Shock protocol), and keep watching breathing and responsiveness. Stay with them.
steps.warn: Do not push organs back in. Do not press on them.
steps.log: Abdominal wound covered with moist dressing

donts: Do not loosen or remove a tourniquet to look at the wound. Removal and conversion are advanced procedures.
Do not cover a tourniquet with clothing or blankets; it must stay visible.
Do not put a tourniquet over the elbow or knee.
Do not use pressure points (pressing on an artery away from the wound) instead of pressing on the wound.
Do not rely on raising the limb or on ice to stop bleeding; there is no evidence they work.
Do not pull out packing or a soaked dressing; press harder or add more on top.
Do not make an improvised tourniquet from thin cord or wire; use a flat band at least 2 inches wide.
Do not press on, or push back, organs showing through a belly wound; cover them loosely with a moist dressing.
evacuate: Evacuate urgently anyone who needed a tourniquet or wound packing.
Evacuate urgently anyone with life-threatening bleeding, even if it is now controlled.
Evacuate urgently if there are signs of shock: confusion, pale cool skin, fast weak pulse, fast breathing.
Evacuate urgently anyone with a belly wound, especially with organs showing.
